words.text: Today you use the word families yourself: spell each member and mark where it changes. Match each word to its meaning, then rewrite sentence openings. Eight more notches up the coyote hole.

reading.text: Read Chapter 15, The Man Who Couldn't Sit Down. Day after day, the partners hunt for gold. Then Jack goes hunting alone. Reread the most dangerous moment, and listen to how calm the telling stays.

cards.title: A note before you read: words from 1963
cards.intro: Chapter 15 has a few lines about Native Californians and Chinese miners. Here is what to know.

items.meaning: The partners see Native women panning for gold, and a prospector calls them Digger Indians. He says they trade their gold for cloth and calls them poor devils, like a bunch of young'uns. Digger was an insult, and calling grown people children is unkind and untrue.

Many Native Californians mined gold in 1848 and 1849. Miwok and Nisenan women washed gold in tightly woven baskets, just as the chapter shows. Then miners took their land and rivers, and disease and violence followed. California's Native population fell from about 150,000 in 1848 to about 30,000 by 1870.

The chapter says Chinese miners moved into camps others had left. That was common. Chinese miners often worked old claims with great care and found gold others had missed. In 1852 California passed a tax of $3 a month on foreign miners that was aimed at them.

cards.note: Sources: Oakland Museum of California; PBS American Experience; Calisphere, University of California.

virtue.name: integrity
virtue.title: The integrity meter
virtue.intro: Think about one moment from Chapter 15.
virtue.moment: The road agent stole Cut-Eye Higgins's linen coat in the holdup. When Jack says it belongs to someone he knows, the man says it gives him a bad conscience to wear it, and he gives it back.
virtue.ask: How much integrity does the road agent show here? Slide to show.
virtue.placeholder: He shows this much integrity because…
virtue.take: Mason's take: more than you might expect from a robber. He doesn't have to give the coat back, and Jack's gun isn't even loaded. But he stole it in the first place. Fleischman lets a bad man do one right thing, and leaves you to weigh it.

art.title: Grizzly Bear
art.alt: A colored print of two large brown grizzly bears in a grassy valley with mountains behind; one stands and one crouches low.
art.look: This hand-colored print was made in 1848 from a painting by John Woodhouse Audubon, for a book about the animals of North America. In the Gold Rush, grizzlies lived all over California. Today the grizzly is on California's state flag, but no wild grizzlies are left in the state.
